tweets.text:
I built my startup in New York, SF, Hawaii, and Japan over the last 60 days (now back in Boston) 🌎👇

Here’s what each place taught me about building.
And LIFE !!

1. New York 🌃

I visited for 5 days for NY Tech Week. And it was ELECTRIC.

From networking events, to hackathons, to a church picnic.
I did it all.

I used to hate networking… UNTIL I stopped treating it as a transaction and rather focused on truly getting to know the other person.

I am typically extroverted, but this week in NY really pushed me beyond my comfort zone, and I’m glad it did.

💡 “Stop networking, start building life-long relationships.”

2. San Francisco 🌉

I was living at the @sorcejobs house on their air mattress for 2 weeks.

Every day was a grind: wake up at 7. work at @fdotinc. leave at 11. sleep. repeat. Their work ethic was intoxicating.

While in SF, I also went viral on X with 9M+ views which helped me to meet some incredible builders like @justinstorre and @hahnbeeIee.

I swear there’s something in the water here.

💡 “Surround yourself with people who inspire you and push your limits.”

3. Hawaii 🏝️

I briefly went back home to visit my family. But for a majority of the time, I was hosting the first-ever @soshiapp Hawaii Builder Program!

Things didn’t go exactly as planned, but overall it was a very rewarding experience.

After NY and SF, we made our biggest strides product-wise during these 2 weeks in an environment where we could truly lock in.

💡 “Get away from the noise to build something great.”

4. Japan 🍣

I was really hesitant to go on this trip to Japan with my girlfriend. I was scared I would “fall behind” in the startup race.

But that’s when I remembered this race is a marathon, not a sprint.

I was working heads down for 6 months straight. 12 hours a day. 7 days a week.

I finally decided to take a week off (even though I still tried to work a little), and this ended up being one of my favorite trips I’ll always remember.

💡 “You don’t need to grind 24/7. You need to start living without regrets.”

HERE’S ONE FINAL LESSON:

Before I left Hawaii, my 96-year-old grandpa told me this:

“Eli, go travel. Many of my favorite memories are from when I traveled all around the world.”

These last 2 months gave me new friends, priceless memories, and a reminder that where you are changes everything. Get out there and explore the world. I promise you won’t regret it.

✈️ Any suggestions where I should go to build next? :)

tweets.text: I've been doing office hours with startups for 20 years now. I must have talked to over a thousand of them. How have I not become bored by it? I think the reason is curiosity. Each startup's idea is different, and it's a puzzle to figure out how to make it work.

Calling Interstellar a terrible movie because it doesn’t align with startup valuation logic is like calling Jurassic Park bad because it lacks a coherent biotech exit strategy.

The water planet scene is not a startup pitch meeting — it’s a dramatic representation of gravitational time dilation, a real concept from general relativity. Christopher Nolan consulted with physicist Kip Thorne to ensure the science was sound. In fact, that sequence is so accurate, it led to published scientific papers.

If you’re upset that ARR would be calculated over 9 minutes, I have great news: nobody gives a fuck about SaaS on the water planet.

Also, the whole point of the mission was to find any habitable planet — not to optimize term sheets and TAM projections. If humanity’s survival comes second to keeping startup multiples inflated, maybe extinction is the right call.

And as for Nolan being broke — pretty sure directing billion-dollar films and winning Oscars beats selling QuickBooks integrations on LinkedIn.

Dumbass
